description: Width tiers for Digital Technologies Years 3-4 (ACARA v9). Covers all 12 descriptors in the Y3-4 band.
subject: Digital Technologies

width_notes.minimum_width: The narrowest honest engagement that satisfies the descriptor's command term. For K-strand standards (explore, recognise): minimum engages with at least one concrete example that genuinely meets the command term. For P-strand standards (define, follow, implement, use, identify, discuss): minimum completes the process or produces the outcome in at least one context. Minimum is not what's easy — it is what's sufficient.
width_notes.typical_width: Full descriptor scope grounded in the most common elaboration cases. What a class that has engaged with the descriptor well would have done. Covers the range of contexts and examples ACARA intended without requiring every elaboration.
width_notes.wider: Enrichment directions that add phenomena, contexts or task variants — not harder versions of the same context. For K-strand: more phenomena and cultural contexts. For P-strand: more task types, audiences or application contexts. First Nations directions from elaborations always included.
width_notes.elaborations: ACARA elaborations are used as the primary source for typical_width and to identify First Nations wider directions. Minimum is set by the descriptor's command term, not by elaboration examples. Wider may infer beyond elaborations where clearly within band territory.

AC9TDI4K01.minimum_width: Explore one digital system and identify its peripherals by category (input, output or storage); describe what purpose the system serves with those peripherals.
AC9TDI4K01.typical_width: Explore and describe a range of digital systems (tablet, desktop, smartphone, laptop) and their peripherals across the input, output and storage categories; explain how different peripheral combinations suit different purposes; demonstrate how adding a peripheral changes what a system can do.
wider: Investigate how digital systems and peripherals are selected for specific professional purposes — for example, the camera and GPS peripherals used by First Nations rangers for land management, or medical imaging devices as specialist output peripherals

Explore how accessibility peripherals (switch controllers, screen readers, braille displays) expand what a digital system can do for different users — discuss how peripheral choice reflects user needs
Investigate how a single device (e.g. a smartphone) functions as a system that integrates multiple input and output peripherals — compare this to a desktop system where peripherals are separate
elaborations: experimenting with a range of peripherals to perform input, output and storage, for example a keyboard, touch screen, mouse, camera and microphone; a monitor, projector, printer or 3D printer; or speaker; or USB drive
adding peripherals to a digital system to expand its functionality, for example connecting a headset to a digital system to participate in an online lesson more effectively

exploring how they can use digital systems differently depending on the task, recognising that many digital systems can perform multiple tasks, for example a student can use a tablet to take photos, record audio and find information to create a presentation

AC9TDI4K02.minimum_width: Explore one example of data being transmitted between digital systems; identify the data type being transmitted and describe what happens.
AC9TDI4K02.typical_width: Explore several examples of different data types (text messages, music streaming, video calls, file sharing) being transmitted between digital systems; describe the sender, data type and receiver in each case; recognise that a network connection is required.
wider: Explore how video call data can be transmitted from remote First Nations communities to city locations — investigate how 3G network coverage limitations affect what data types can be reliably transmitted and what this means for remote communities

Investigate how data transmission underpins real-time services (online gaming, emergency services, live weather data) — explore what types of data are transmitted and why transmission speed or reliability matters in each case
Explore how the same data (e.g. a school assignment) can be transmitted in different ways (email attachment, shared folder, USB drive) and discuss the differences in how and when the data moves
elaborations: exploring examples of different types of data that can be transferred between digital systems, for example streaming music or making a video call to a friend using a smartphone

exploring how data (video call) can be transmitted from a remote community to a city location, for example looking at how many First Nations Australian communities in areas classified as remote rely on 3G network coverage, limiting the use of video calls

AC9TDI4K03.minimum_width: Recognise at least three types of data (e.g. numbers, text, symbols, images); give one example of the same data shown in two different representations.
AC9TDI4K03.typical_width: Recognise data types (numbers, text, symbols, images) and explain how the same data can be represented in different ways; explain why some representations suit particular purposes better than others across several examples (numerals vs words for calculation, icons for multilingual audiences, symbols for universal communication).
wider: Investigate how First Nations Australian rock paintings and ancient engravings encode ethnobotanical knowledge — compare how image-based representation of plant and animal data differs in purpose and structure from modern classification text

Explore how geographic data (a location) can be represented as coordinates, a street address, a map pin and a place name — discuss which representation suits navigation, database storage, verbal communication and visual display respectively

Investigate how emoji as a representation system sits at the boundary of symbols and images — explore what kinds of meaning can and cannot be reliably encoded in emoji and how representation choice shapes communication
elaborations: describing different types of data and how they can be used, for example numbers, letters, symbols and pictures

explaining how the same data can be represented in different ways and why some representations are better than others in certain contexts, for example four vs 4 vs IV vs I I I I vs quatre and that numerals are better for calculation than words
explaining that the same information can be represented differently, for example the term 'stop' can also be represented with an octagon-shaped red sign or a hand icon

identifying rock paintings and other cultural expressions to understand that images are used to encode and represent ethnobotanical knowledge, for example the representation of plant use in the Kimberley cave paintings and ancient engravings including important data on medicinal and food plant classification and their usable parts

AC9TDI4P01.minimum_width: Given a familiar problem, use a given design criterion and co-create one user story using a template that identifies a user, need and purpose.
AC9TDI4P01.typical_width: Define problems across different contexts using given design criteria and co-created user stories; apply the user story template to problems of different types (entertainment, information access, communication, monitoring); check that criteria are consistent with the user story.
wider: Define problems from the perspective of users in First Nations community contexts — for example, a student wanting to explore remote neighbouring countries, or ranger groups needing to monitor animal populations using GPS; discuss how context shapes what criteria and user stories include
Define a problem with multiple users who have different needs — explore how user stories for different users may conflict and how design criteria accommodate or prioritise different needs
Co-create user stories for a problem involving non-human or collective users (e.g. a school library, a ranger group) — discuss what changes when the 'user' is not an individual
elaborations: recognising a range of familiar problems and defining achievable solutions using given design criteria, for example buying presents for family members within a specified budget
using responses to guiding questions to write a user story, for example a family member wants a way of entertaining their puppy when they are at school to stop it digging holes
co-creating a user story using a template such as 'A has so that ', for example 'a sports team wants to access league rankings online so that they can see their progress'

developing a problem statement for collecting and managing information, for example how First Nations Australians rangers could monitor animal populations, such as local marine turtles, using global positioning systems (GPS)
co-creating user stories about exploring hard-to-reach locations, for example a school student wants to explore neighbouring countries classified as remote to compare how people live

AC9TDI4P02.minimum_width: Follow an algorithm that includes at least two of the three structures (sequencing, a comparison-based branch, or fixed-count iteration) and describe what each structure does in plain language.
AC9TDI4P02.typical_width: Follow and describe algorithms involving all three structures (sequencing, comparison operators as branches, fixed-count iteration) across different contexts; use representations such as step lists or diagrams; explain what changes with each iteration and trace both paths of a branch for different input values.
wider: Describe algorithms that encode First Nations Australian protocols with strict ordering and conditional rules — for example, ranger procedures with IF/THEN decision rules and repeated survey steps; discuss how algorithm structures formalise real-world decision-making
Follow and describe an algorithm that combines iteration and branching — explain how repeating steps interact with conditional checks (e.g. 'keep checking each item until condition is met')

Compare two algorithms that solve the same problem differently — identify the structural differences (different branch conditions, different number of iterations) and discuss which is more efficient or appropriate for the context
elaborations: following the steps and decisions of algorithms and knowing what step they are up to, for example following rules to form the past tense of regular verbs such as 'create' to 'created', 'try' to 'tried' and 'cook' to 'cooked' and checking off items on a list as they are completed
describing algorithms using representations such as a list of steps or a diagram, for example drawing a diagram of a recipe involving decisions

understanding there can be more than one sequence of steps to solve a problem, some are better than others, and the steps should be unambiguous, for example describing 2 different ways to get to the same location
describing the decisions needed to solve a problem, including numerical and text comparisons, for example if the UV index is above 3, put on sunscreen and a hat
describing algorithms that repeat steps a fixed number of times, for example calculating multiplication using repeated addition, where the sum changes in each iteration

AC9TDI4P03.minimum_width: Generate at least two different design ideas for a simple problem, communicate each idea so a peer can understand what it proposes, and state which better meets the user's need with one reason.
AC9TDI4P03.typical_width: Generate, communicate and compare multiple design ideas across different problem contexts; discuss whether each idea meets the user stories and design criteria; accept all ideas as possibilities before comparing; provide reasons for judgements that reference the criteria.
wider: Generate and compare design ideas for a problem with a First Nations Australian community context — explore how ideas that seem obvious for a mainstream context may not suit the actual users, and how the design criteria reflect this
Ideate for a problem where different users have conflicting needs — generate ideas that try to satisfy multiple user stories and compare how well each design balances competing requirements
Compare designs where no single idea fully meets all criteria — practise making a reasoned choice between imperfect options and articulating the trade-off
elaborations: brainstorming possible design ideas and discussing these with their peers, for example sketching different ideas for a computer game
discussing whether the needs identified from the user story are met by generated design ideas, for example comparing design ideas in pairs for encouraging people to recycle

ideating multiple design ideas and comparing them against user stories, for example as a class, discussing the needs identified from the user story and brainstorming multiple design ideas (accepting all suggestions as possibilities)

AC9TDI4P04.minimum_width: Write and run a visual program that implements at least two of the three control structures (sequence, branching, iteration) and accepts user or environmental input in at least one context.
AC9TDI4P04.typical_width: Implement simple algorithms as visual programs using all three control structures and user or environmental input across different task contexts (games, quiz programs, simulations, calculation tools); test programs and confirm they perform as expected.
wider: Implement a program that encodes a First Nations Australian ranger protocol using IF/THEN statements — for example, a training program that guides a user through the correct procedure for handling an injured native animal
Write a program that uses both a loop and a branch together — explore how the structures interact when a condition is checked inside a repeating sequence
Implement the same algorithm in two different visual programming environments — compare how each environment represents the same logic and discuss what changes and what stays the same
elaborations: writing and editing programs to solve simple problems using branching and simple iteration in a visual programming environment, for example helping a user understand multiplication by displaying the repeated addition in order
writing programs that take input from the user or environment, for example asking the user for their name and displaying it or sensing the temperature from the environment to make a decision
writing programs that make decisions involving comparison, for example comparing whether the temperature is above 25 degrees Celsius to label the weather hot or cold
writing programs that repeat one or more steps a fixed number of times, for example writing a program that displays repetitive song lyrics, such as in 'Ten in the bed'
running and testing a program to check it performs as expected, for example a character: 1. moves forward 2. turns left 3. moves forward

implementing a program that demonstrates the strict routines and techniques followed by First Nations Australian ranger groups when caring for or handling specific native animals, for example using IF and THEN statements to create a training manual, such as: IF  is injured THEN the ranger will

AC9TDI4P05.minimum_width: Describe one existing or student-created digital solution and discuss whether it meets at least one design criterion or user story element.
AC9TDI4P05.typical_width: Discuss how existing and student-created digital solutions satisfy design criteria and user stories across different contexts (maps, online ordering systems, interactive directories, student-created games and tools); identify what criteria are met and where solutions fall short; give reasons grounded in the criteria.
wider: Evaluate a digital solution designed for a First Nations context (e.g. a ranger monitoring system) against design criteria reflecting that community's needs — discuss how solutions that work in mainstream contexts may not meet context-specific criteria

Evaluate a solution from both the designer's perspective and a different user's perspective — discuss how the same solution can be judged differently depending on who is evaluating and what their needs are
Discuss a solution that meets stated criteria but fails in actual use — explore the gap between designed criteria and real user experience
elaborations: describing the way familiar digital systems allow the user to perform tasks, for example discussing how a family member could place an order online for something they cannot buy locally

discussing how a digital solution meets the different needs of users, for example how maps help people to locate places in the community or interactive store directories help shoppers to find a particular store in a shopping centre
making judgements on their digital solutions against the design criteria and user stories, for example how high their friends score in the game they created to help them learn what is recyclable
reflecting on how the systems in the school help it run, for example how the librarian keeps track of books borrowed

AC9TDI4P06.minimum_width: Use core features of one digital tool to create content for a purpose, following at least two agreed conventions (e.g. appropriate file naming, correct folder placement, safe search steps).
AC9TDI4P06.typical_width: Use core features of common digital tools to create, locate and communicate content across different formats (presentations, documents, research tasks); apply agreed conventions consistently including safe search steps, information hierarchy, and appropriate use of autocomplete features.
wider: Create content using a tool that is unfamiliar — apply conventions learned in known tools and reflect on which transferred and which required adjustment; discuss what makes conventions tool-specific versus general
Create content intended for an audience beyond the classroom (e.g. a presentation for parents or a guide for a younger class) — discuss how agreed conventions change depending on audience and purpose
Design and apply a file organisation system for a class-wide project — create folders and naming conventions that allow others to find content without guidance; evaluate the system's effectiveness
elaborations: discussing and creating as a class a set of steps they need to follow to safely find information online
using an online search engine to find suitable sources to create and communicate information, following agreed steps, for example creating a presentation on life cycles
grouping, naming and itemising objects using a logical hierarchy, for example creating a section of a virtual library or virtual supermarket using folders and files
using autocomplete features in text authoring tools; for example, using suggestions in a word processor to complete words or sentences, or using predictive text in SMS or messaging apps

AC9TDI4P07.minimum_width: Use a digital tool to share content with an agreed audience and contribute to one collaborative planning task, following agreed behaviours.
AC9TDI4P07.typical_width: Use core features of digital tools to share content appropriately, plan tasks and collaborate with peers across different contexts (shared folders, surveys, group documents); demonstrate agreed behaviours including taking turns, respecting others' contributions, and keeping personal information private.
wider: Collaborate with students from another class or year level using digital tools — reflect on how agreed behaviours need to be explicitly re-established with new collaborators and in new tools
Plan and administer a class survey using a digital tool — analyse results collaboratively and use them to make a group decision; discuss how digital tools support group decision-making at scale

Demonstrate safe sharing by comparing what information should be included or excluded when sharing a holiday adventure publicly versus privately — discuss how audience determines what is appropriate to share
elaborations: using an agreed folder to make it easy for students to collaborate on shared content in a group project
demonstrating safe sharing of content with a select audience, for example sharing a holiday adventure without revealing exact dates, specific names or other personal information

listening to others when participating in online environments to share content, for example respecting the rights of others by taking turns to suggest and add words or images to a factual slide deck to share with the teacher
interacting cooperatively in a group in an online environment to plan and complete a task, for example writing and responding to others' views on canteen products

using digital tools to plan an event as a class, for example jointly creating a class survey to help plan an end-of-year party, where responses conform to the class's accepted behavioural expectations

AC9TDI4P08.minimum_width: Access a school account using a memorised password and explain one characteristic that makes the password both memorable and hard to guess.
AC9TDI4P08.typical_width: Access a school account independently using a memorised password; explain what makes a password secure (unpredictable, not based on easily known personal details) and memorable (uses familiar but unrelated elements); apply a password-creation technique (e.g. three unrelated words) to a new example.
wider: Investigate why commonly chosen passwords (names, birthdays, 'password123') are weak — connect to the concept of digital identity from AC9TDI4P09, exploring how personal information stored online could help someone guess a password

Explore passphrase-style passwords and compare their security and memorability to single complex words with symbols — explain why a longer phrase of random words can be more secure despite being easier to remember

Limited width — password security at this year band does not vary significantly across more contexts. Extension involves going further into multi-factor authentication or password manager concepts, which are beyond the Y3-4 band.
elaborations: recalling their school username and password from memory to login to a school laptop or desktop
explaining how keeping a password secret prevents others from accessing their data, for example how their work is saved in their account and can only be accessed using their secret password
exploring techniques to create an easy to remember and hard to guess password, for example creating a password using 3 unrelated but easy to remember words
AC9TDI4P08.width_notes: Limited width — password concepts at this band have a thin range of contexts. One First Nations connection is available via the digital identity link but the concept does not significantly vary across more phenomena.

AC9TDI4P09.minimum_width: Identify personal data stored in one online account they use and name one risk associated with that data being accessible.
AC9TDI4P09.typical_width: Identify personal data stored and shared across different online account types (school cloud storage, gaming accounts, communication apps); explain how stored data forms part of a digital identity; discuss risks associated with data being accessible to different audiences.
wider: Analyse photographs of themselves, friends or fictional characters to identify what location, habit or home information could be inferred from the image — discuss how images are personal data with embedded information that reveals more than intended

Investigate how data shared for one purpose creates unexpected risks in another context — for example, a gaming nickname and play patterns being visible to all players, or school cloud documents being accessible to the teacher

Discuss the concept of a digital footprint — how personal data stored across multiple accounts collectively reveals detailed information about a person's life even when no single account contains everything
elaborations: identifying the personal data stored in accounts they use at school and at home and who has access to it, for example documents in their school cloud storage are accessible by the teacher, or their nickname in their online gaming accounts is visible to all players

discussing how personal data stored in online accounts forms a person's digital identity and can reveal detailed information about people, for example looking at photographs of themselves, friends or fictional characters that reveal details about a person's location, habits or home
